title: Open and Close in the Right Order
oneLiner: Open a list of resources, do the work, and close every resource that was opened, newest first, even when opening one of them or the work itself fails.
keyTakeaway: Clean-up must run on every path: success, a failure while acquiring, and a failure during the work. Release only what was actually acquired, in reverse order. With a number of resources known only at run time, keep a list and dispose it backwards in a finally block (C#), or let contextlib.ExitStack do exactly that (Python).
explanation:
Write RunSteps(names, failOn, log). It must open one Resource per name, in order, then add "work" to the log, then close the resources in reverse order. Opening a resource logs "open name" and closing it logs "close name"; the Resource type is provided and does the logging. The test can make things fail: if failOn is one of the names, opening that resource throws, and if failOn is "work", your code must throw after logging "work" (C#: throw new InvalidOperationException("work failed"); Python: raise RuntimeError("work failed")). Either way, every resource that was opened must still be closed, newest first, and the exception must reach the caller. The checker returns the log, plus "error: message" if an exception came out.

So names ["a", "b", "c"] with failOn "c" gives ["open a", "open b", "close b", "close a", "error: cannot open c"]: c was never opened, so it isn't closed, and "work" never happens.

In C#, Resource implements IDisposable and its constructor opens it: new Resource(name, failOn, log). A fixed number of resources would be a stack of using statements, but here the count varies, so add each one to a List<Resource> as it opens and, in a finally block, dispose them from the last to the first. In Python, Resource(name, fail_on, log) is a context manager that opens in __enter__; use "with ExitStack() as stack:" and stack.enter_context(Resource(...)) for each name, and ExitStack closes them in reverse for you.

testCases.expectedJson: ["open a", "open b", "open c", "work", "close c", "close b", "close a", "error: work failed"]
["open a", "open b", "close b", "close a", "error: cannot open c"]
["open conn", "open tx", "close tx", "close conn", "error: cannot open lock"]

visualizationSteps.message: Three resources to open, and the test says opening c will fail.
Opening c throws. The work never runs, and c was never opened, so it must not be closed.
The finally block (or ExitStack) closes what was opened, newest first: b...
...then a. The exception then carries on to the caller, which logs "error: cannot open c".

complexity.note: Each of the n resources is opened once and closed once; the list (or ExitStack) remembers up to n opened resources so they can be closed in reverse.
